tagline: Desert basins and mountain turns along an old overland travel corridor
intro: East of Fallon, U.S. 50 narrows from four lanes to two and crosses the Basin and Range landscape of desert valleys and mountain ranges. Above Austin, hairpin turns and steep grades climb toward Austin Summit in the Toiyabe Range. The mountainous section east of Ely has Nevada Scenic Byway designation, with Ward Charcoal Ovens and Great Basin National Park among its listed attractions.

The highway was built largely along the Lincoln Highway’s route, itself following a corridor used by the Pony Express. The routes are not identical: east of Middlegate, they use different passes through the Desatoya Mountains before rejoining west of Austin. In July 1986, Life magazine called U.S. 50 the Loneliest Road in America. White Pine County officials and state authorities turned the criticism into a promotion for desert scenery, history and solitude. The Nevada Department of Transportation adopted the nickname in its highway logs and installed custom Highway 50 markers along the route.

From Fallon, the eastbound drive passes Sand Mountain before reaching Austin and the petroglyphs near Hickison Summit. Eureka comes next, then Ely, where U.S. 50 leaves the older routes toward Salt Lake City. Beyond Ely, Connors Pass reaches 7,729 feet, the highway’s highest point in Nevada, before the road enters Utah northeast of Baker.
notice: Above Austin, the highway climbs through hairpin turns toward Austin Summit.

moments.title: Sand Mountain
moments.text: Sand Mountain rises 600 feet beside U.S. 50, twenty miles east of Fallon. The two-mile-long dune is made from sand originating in ancient Lake Lahontan, which largely dried up 9,000 years ago. It is a singing dune, and the surrounding recreation area is the only home of the critically imperiled Sand Mountain blue butterfly. The ruins of the Pony Express’s Sand Springs Station are also within the recreation area. The entire sand field covers 3.25 square miles, and the Bureau of Land Management manages the recreation area.

moments.title: Austin
moments.text: The town itself occupies the western slopes of the Toiyabe Range, with U.S. 50 passing through at 6,575 feet. One sack of flour became a traveling fundraiser launched from Austin in 1864. Reuel Colt Gridley’s flour was sold and resold for the U.S. Sanitary Commission, which aided wounded Union soldiers. The auctions began in Austin, spread through Nevada and continued in the East, with support from Mark Twain. The campaign eventually raised more than $250,000. Gridley’s 1863 store is a one-story granite building in Upper Austin; its present exterior dates from a renovation in about 1985.

moments.title: Hickison Summit
moments.text: A half-mile trail at Hickison Petroglyph Recreation Area passes multiple panels of rock carvings and high-desert plants. The site lies at 6,500 feet on the western edge of Monitor Valley, east of Austin along U.S. 50. Views from the trail include the Toquima and Toiyabe ranges and Big Smoky Valley. The wider summit area contains prehistoric hunting and living sites as well as later mining camps and ranches. Pony Express and Overland Stage routes passed through the area, as did trails used by nineteenth-century explorers John C. Frémont and James H. Simpson.
moments.notice: The trail passes petroglyph panels and offers views of the Toquima and Toiyabe ranges.
